steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Because of very-large-scale integration (VLSI) technology, the group of Yannis Tsividis at Columbia University has been looking again at the design of analog and hybrid computers, using a standard CMOS process. They developed two VLSI chips. The first one is an 80th-order analog computer (250 nm) made by Glenn Cowan in 2005. The second one is a 4th-order hybrid computer (65 nm) that Ning Guo developed in 2015. Both of the chips are aimed at energy-efficient ODE/PDE applications. Glenn's chip has 16 macros, and in them there are 25 analog computing blocks, which are integrators, multipliers, fanouts and a few nonlinear blocks. Ning's chip has one macro block with 26 computing blocks, including integrators, multipliers, fanouts, ADCs, SRAMs and DACs. The ADC+SRAM+DAC chain makes it possible to generate arbitrary nonlinear functions, with the SRAM block storing the data of the nonlinear function.

- Results
  - about 1–2 orders of magnitude advantage in solution time and energy, accuracy within 5%
  - promise for energy-efficient approximate computing
  - 2016: research team builds compiler to solve differential equations with analog circuits
- Neuromorphic computing
  - 2021: researchers show spiking neural networks can work with analog neuromorphic computers
- THE ANALOG THING (THAT)
  - anabrid GmbH (Germany), from 2021; small, low-cost, mainly educational and scientific use
  - company also building analog mainframes and hybrid computers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Because of very-large-scale integration (VLSI) technology, the group of Yannis Tsividis at Columbia University has been looking again at the design of analog and hybrid computers, using a standard CMOS process. They developed two VLSI chips. The first one is an 80th-order analog computer (250 nm) made by Glenn Cowan in 2005. The second one is a 4th-order hybrid computer (65 nm) that Ning Guo developed in 2015. Both of the chips are aimed at energy-efficient ODE/PDE applications. Glenn's chip has 16 macros, and in them there are 25 analog computing blocks, which are integrators, multipliers, fanouts and a few nonlinear blocks. Ning's chip has one macro block with 26 computing blocks, including integrators, multipliers, fanouts, ADCs, SRAMs and DACs. The ADC+SRAM+DAC chain makes it possible to generate arbitrary nonlinear functions, with the SRAM block storing the data of the nonlinear function. Experiments in the related publications showed that the VLSI analog/hybrid computers had an advantage of about 1–2 orders of magnitude in both solution time and energy, and the accuracy was within 5%. This shows that analog/hybrid computing techniques are promising for energy-efficient approximate computing. Also, in 2016 a team of researchers developed a compiler that solves differential equations using analog circuits.

Analog computers are also used for neuromorphic computing. In 2021 a group of researchers showed that a spiking neural network, which is a specific type of artificial neural network, was able to work with analog neuromorphic computers.

The German company anabrid GmbH started to produce THE ANALOG THING (THAT for short) in 2021. It is a small analog computer with a low cost, and it is mainly for educational and scientific use. The company is also building analog mainframes and hybrid computers.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the development of very-large-scale integration (VLSI) technology, Yannis Tsividis' group at Columbia University has been revisiting the design of analog/hybrid computers in a standard CMOS process. Two VLSI chips have been developed: an 80th-order analog computer (250 nm) by Glenn Cowan[1] in 2005[2] and a 4th-order hybrid computer (65 nm) developed by Ning Guo in 2015,[3] both aimed at energy-efficient ODE/PDE applications. Glenn's chip contains 16 macros, in which there are 25 analog computing blocks, namely integrators, multipliers, fanouts and a few nonlinear blocks. Ning's chip contains one macro block with 26 computing blocks, including integrators, multipliers, fanouts, ADCs, SRAMs and DACs. Arbitrary nonlinear function generation is made possible by the ADC+SRAM+DAC chain, where the SRAM block stores the nonlinear function data. Experiments in the related publications showed that VLSI analog/hybrid computers had about 1–2 orders of magnitude advantage in both solution time and energy while achieving accuracy within 5%, which points to the promise of analog/hybrid computing techniques for energy-efficient approximate computing. In 2016, a team of researchers developed a compiler to solve differential equations using analog circuits.[4]

Analog computers are also used in neuromorphic computing, and in 2021 a group of researchers showed that a specific type of artificial neural network, the spiking neural network, was able to work with analog neuromorphic computers.[5]

In 2021, the German company anabrid GmbH began producing THE ANALOG THING (abbreviated THAT), a small, low-cost analog computer mainly for educational and scientific use.[6] The company is also building analog mainframes and hybrid computers.
